title: CS Quest 6.2 · Made for everyone (Accessibility, usability, bias)
name: Made for everyone (Accessibility, usability, bias)
summary: Two Play steps. Play A: students audit a game with four real settings, then Design Lab in Inside the Machine (a bright-sun user, face unlock tested on a group that all looked alike, a controller for one hand size) and recommend changes that help more than one group. Play B: Fair Data in Data Detective, four cases of biased samples and who was missing.
iCan: test the usability and accessibility of a game and recommend an improvement that helps more than one group
spot bias in how something was designed or tested, and say who was missing
materials: Accessibility Audit sheet printable (one per student)
persona cards and a paper remote (for the twin)
doNow: Close your eyes for ten seconds while a neighbor plays any game with the sound off. Write what you missed, and who else would miss it.
plan: Explore: the Settings panel and the face-unlock story
Play A: audit sheet, then Design Lab (10) · Play B: Fair Data (8)

warmup.why: the unit opener (6.1 had no warm-up), one retrieval item from 6.1, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 6.1

do: Open any game's Settings panel on the projector and read the switches out loud: motion, captions, read-aloud, text size, speed, assist, contrast, color cues, left-handed, graphics. Turn contrast up and ask who needs it in bright sun.
Open Inside the Machine at Design Lab (Open game at this chapter), read the first brief with the class, and point at the user quote: that quote is the analysis every recommendation must come from.
say: Designing for people at the edges makes things better for everyone: a high-contrast mode made for low vision is the mode everyone uses in the sun.
Bias is when a technology works worse for some people because of how it was built or tested. Face unlock that fails for darker skin was most likely tested on a group that all looked alike.
ask: Who is each switch for, and who else does it help? And for the face unlock: who was missing from the testing group?
explore.afterAsk: Write two headings on the board: made for / also helps, and who was missing. Students fill both from the game's verdicts during Play.
explore.bigIdea: Good design starts with how real people use a thing, including the people who were not in the room when it was tested.

play.goal: the audit sheet with 4 settings, then 2 briefs

steps: Each student opens Robo Route at a level they have already beaten and tries 4 settings from the audit sheet one at a time: captions, text size, contrast, left-handed.
For each setting they circle could I still play (yes, kind of, no) and write who it helps and who else.
They write two improvements for the game, each with the user it comes from.

play.solo: one device per student; at the end of Play A each student swaps audit sheets with a neighbor and adds one improvement from the other sheet
lookFors: a recommendation with no user behind it: ask which quote or which audit result it comes from
in Fair Data, a fix that drops the missing group instead of surveying it: the last case wants the two extra groups named
play.misconception: Students think a biased system was built by biased people on purpose; the point of the lesson is that bias usually comes from who was in the testing group and who was not, so the fix is to test with more kinds of people.
earlyFinishers: earn 3 stars on every brief and case
help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Which setting surprised you by helping you?
Who was missing from the testing group in the face-unlock case, and what would you change about the test?
showMe: One student shows the last Fair Data case on the projector: which two groups they chose to survey and why.

exit.frame: ___ would help ___ and also ___. The people missing from the testing were ___.

rubric.line: Bias and accessibility: who was missing, and the effect
levels: Names a group that was left out, or a thing that does not work for someone
Names the missing group and the effect on them
Names the missing group, the effect, and a change to how it should be tested

levels: Names an improvement and who it helps, from how they use the device
Names an improvement, who it was made for and who else it helps, with the evidence: a quote, a test or an audit result

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: audit sheet with icons and a three-face scale; read-aloud on for the briefs
Fair Data case 1 on the projector with the class before solo play
stretch: all five briefs, then audit a second game
write the survey plan for the last Fair Data case: which groups, how many of each, what question

unpluggedTwin.title: Design for Sam, and who was missing
materials: persona cards: a Sam who sees little, a Sam who hears little, a Sam who uses one hand, a Sam who is five, a Sam in bright sun
a paper remote (a drawn controller with six big buttons)
testing-group cards: a face-unlock test, a best-lunch survey, a voice helper test, each with the list of who was asked
steps: Each pair gets one persona card and the paper remote. They mark every button and screen that would be hard for their Sam and redraw the remote: bigger buttons, a shape next to every color, a one-hand layout, a high-contrast mode.
Pairs swap remotes with a pair who had a different Sam and add one change the other pair's Sam needs.
Each pair takes one testing-group card, circles who is missing from the list of people asked, and writes the two groups they would add and why.
Share: which change helps more than one Sam, and which missing group surprised you?

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: close your eyes for ten seconds while a neighbor plays any game with the sound off; write what you missed and who else would miss it.

Play Inside the Machine, chapter Design Lab (Pro), for 10 minutes, the first 4 on the audit sheet; then Data Detective, chapter Fair Data, for 8 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play A and Play B. If a game asks, the quest code is 6 2 0 0 in both games. Goal: 2 briefs and 3 cases. Playing signed out is fine; students swap audit sheets with a neighbor and add one idea.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it with the audit sheets.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: Close your eyes for ten seconds while a neighbor plays any game with the sound off. Write what you missed, and who else would miss it.

Big idea: Good design starts with how real people use a thing, including the people who were not in the room when it was tested.

We will talk about:
- Which setting surprised you by helping you?
- Who was missing from the testing group in the face-unlock case?

steps.title: Warm-up (live)
steps.body: Five quick questions. Your teacher shows them on the projector or starts them live.

steps.title: Play A: Design Lab
steps.body:
First 4 minutes: the audit sheet. Open a level you already beat, try 4 settings from the gear, and write who each one helps and who else.
Then Design Lab. Goal: 2 briefs. Stretch: all 5, then 3 stars. Every change you pick must come from the user's quote.
If the game asks for a quest code, it is 6 2 0 0.
Before Play B, swap audit sheets with a neighbor and add one improvement from theirs to yours.

steps.title: Play B: Fair Data
steps.body:
Four cases about data that left people out. Goal: 3 cases. Stretch: all 4, then 3 stars.
In the last case, pick the two extra groups you would survey.
If the game asks for a quest code, it is 6 2 0 0 here too.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about bias and designing for everyone.

steps.title: In your own words
steps.body:
Recommend one improvement to a game or device. Say who it helps, who else it helps, and who was missing when it was designed or tested.
Frame: ___ would help ___ and also ___. The people missing from the testing were ___.
